shortDescription.text: Transaction signing for 3 chain(s) relies on elliptic-curve signatures

fullDescription.text: The wallet's message definitions cover Bitcoin, Cardano, Ethereum and EVM chains. These chains authorize transactions with ECDSA, Ed25519, Schnorr (BIP-340), which Shor's algorithm breaks on a cryptographically relevant quantum computer. A wallet cannot move a chain to post-quantum signatures on its own: the chain has to adopt a scheme first. Follow each chain's post-quantum roadmap, avoid public-key reuse, and keep signers ready to add post-quantum signature schemes as chains adopt them. Keep the signing layer crypto-agile per chain (algorithm identifiers in messages and storage, room for larger keys and signatures) and track each chain's post-quantum proposals, so that a new scheme can be added when a chain activates it. This is a forward-looking risk that depends on the arrival of a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC). No such computer is publicly known to exist today; the timeline is uncertain. It is not a present-day exploitable vulnerability. Chains are recognized…

shortDescription.text: Quantum-vulnerable ECDSA: firmware and boot verification (root of trust) (3 file(s))

fullDescription.text: 7 reference(s) to ECDSA across 3 file(s), e.g. src/bootloader/bootloader.c:537. Role, judged from paths, function names and nearby code: firmware and boot verification (root of trust). These public keys are fixed in the bootloader or the device: with a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) an attacker forges a firmware signature, and replacing the keys needs a bootloader update in the field. Plan a hybrid firmware signature (the classical one plus ML-DSA or SLH-DSA, both required) and the path to ship the new keys in a bootloader update.
